# Overview {.unnumbered}

{{< include _caution.qmd >}}

## The question

Children need far fewer exposures to learn a noun late in development than early on. In the
accelerating-accumulator analysis of children's vocabulary (Frank, *Children, but not language
models, show accelerating returns in word learning*, arXiv 2026), the estimated cumulative
exposures at acquisition fall from a median of about 1,900 for nouns learned at 16–20 months to
about 170 for nouns learned at 28–32 months. Language models trained on comparable input show no
such decline.

One candidate explanation is a feedback loop: what a learner already knows helps it work out what
each new utterance is about, so it extracts more from each exposure, so it learns more. This book
asks a narrow version of that question:

> In a world with the referential statistics of children's input, can knowledge-dependent
> inference make a new noun cheaper by an order of magnitude, and if so, under what conditions?

## Why a new model

Two earlier pieces of work motivate this one.

- **Simulations of the Frank, Goodman & Tenenbaum (2009) word-learning model.** Knowledge made new
  words about 2.4× cheaper, through inference about the speaker's intended referent. But the effect
  came from relieving a penalty the model places on any named object that is present but not
  mentioned, which is a poor description of a living room. Removing the penalty gave a better
  learner and no acceleration.
- **Contrastive vision–language models trained on BabyView egocentric video.** About 10% of
  frame–utterance pairs were judged referentially aligned by an automatic annotator, and 7% had a
  spoken referent noun. Training only on aligned pairs was 20× to 34× more data-efficient than
  training on everything. Attempts to have the model find those pairs itself did not work.

So the leverage seems to lie in knowing *which* utterances are about something present, and the
model here makes that an explicit variable.

## The model in one paragraph

Each utterance has a hidden **gate** $G$: is it about something present? If so, it has a **topic**
$Z$, the object it names. Referential utterances come in **bouts**, with persistence $\lambda$. An
object that is present but not mentioned is neutral: it is never evidence against that object
having a name. Knowledge can then help in two ways. It can prune candidates, because objects that
already have names are unlikely referents for a new noun. And it can inform the gate, because a
known noun spoken nearby while its object is present signals that the current stretch of talk is
about the scene. @sec-model gives the full specification.

## What we found

1. **Pruning alone is a small effect.** When the nouns a learner knows are the ones more frequent
   than the new noun, ruling them out makes the new noun at most about 1.4× cheaper
   (@sec-single-noun).
2. **Without bouts, knowledge says nothing about the gate.** With one noun per utterance and
   referential status independent across utterances, every cue built from knowledge has a gain of
   exactly 1 (@sec-bouts).
3. **The ceiling grows as naming gets rarer and scenes get more cluttered.** Telling the learner
   which uses are referential is worth about 2× when 10% of a noun's uses are referential, and about
   28× at 0.5% with 8 objects in view (@sec-bouts).
4. **With long bouts, knowledge reaches most of that ceiling.** At a 1% referential rate with 8
   objects in view and bout persistence 0.95, a noun costs about 2,550 exposures with nothing known
   and about 250 with 64% of noun tokens known: a 10× decline, the same size as children's.
5. **The same conditions make first words very expensive.** Whether a learner can earn its first
   words, so that the loop starts, is the main open question (@sec-next).

## Status and handoff

**Done.** Stage-1 analysis with *clamped* knowledge: the learner is handed a set of known nouns, and
we measure how much cheaper a fixed new noun becomes. Exact posteriors throughout, paired
simulations, and the analytic formulas checked against simulation.

**Not done.** A developmental ladder where knowledge is earned; topics that persist within a bout;
several nouns per utterance; calibration of the referential rate, bout persistence and clutter from
BabyView; and the BabyView model experiment that the theory is meant to design. @sec-next lays these
out in order.

## Reading guide

| chapter | contents |
|---|---|
| @sec-model | every symbol and equation |
| @sec-single-noun | evidence per exposure for one new noun; what pruning and a referential cue buy |
| @sec-bouts | how bouts let knowledge reach the gate; the size of the ceiling; comparison with children |
| @sec-next | open questions, the planned next analyses, and decisions already made |

**How results are measured.** The primary readout is the number of exposures a learner needs before
the posterior on a noun's true referent first exceeds 0.5. Knowledge is manipulated by hand, and the
*gain* is the ratio of exposures with no knowledge to exposures with knowledge, on the same data. We
do not use the per-word slope statistic $\kappa$ from the developmental paper here. In the earlier
simulations it did not separate learners with and without feedback, which we take to mean that it
was not measuring learning appropriately for Bayesian threshold learners.

## Reproducing

From the repository root:

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/python -m ipykernel install --user --name vlm-acceleration
cd theory
for s in run_single_noun run_bouts run_ceiling run_lowrho; do ../.venv/bin/python $s.py; done
cd ../book && ./render.sh
```

The second line registers a Jupyter kernel that points at the repo's virtual environment; the
chapters name it in their front matter so that they never run under some other Python.

The four scripts take about a minute in total on a laptop with 10 or more cores and write the CSV
files in `theory/results/` that every table and figure here reads. They are deterministic: rerunning
them reproduces the committed results exactly.
